concepts.objective: Specify a treatment, comparison, population and outcome, and distinguish setting a treatment from observing its value.
Calculate a population-average contrast between two intervention values, stating direction, units and target population without assigning it to each individual.
Explain confounding and standardize stratum-specific outcomes to a common population only under an adequate pre-treatment adjustment set, overlap and consistency.
Distinguish effect identification under explicit causal and design assumptions from estimation with finite data and from generalization to another population.

claims.proposition: An intervention replaces the assignment mechanism of the selected variable; observing a value generally leaves its causes and selection process in place.

source_refs.locator: Sections 3.2 and 6.3, intervention definitions and Example 6.10

claims.proposition: An average causal effect contrasts expected outcomes under two specified interventions in a specified population; for a binary outcome a risk difference is expressed in probability or percentage points.

A valid adjustment formula combines conditional outcome distributions with the same pre-intervention covariate distribution for each treatment. Validity depends on the causal structure, not merely on including many variables.

claims.proposition: An intervention distribution may be determined by observational data together with a causal model and valid adjustment assumptions; an observational association alone need not determine it.

claims.proposition: Reference counts and assessment cases in this pack are authored teaching data. Interactive experiment outcomes are deterministically recomputed from the released model and learner settings. Ratios, differences and weighted sums use declared denominators and target weights. Generation fidelity and withholding criteria are declared teaching-model rules, not empirical guarantees or textbook claims about a particular generator.

resources.text: For eligible rehabilitation patients, compare assignment to programme A with assignment to programme B. Success means reach the mobility target at six weeks; choosing a programme is not the same as being assigned one.
Worked example

For eligible rehabilitation patients, let A=1 mean assignment to the specified six-week programme and A=0 mean assignment to its stated comparison. Define success and the follow-up time. The notation do(A=1) means actively setting assignment to 1, not selecting existing records with A=1.

People choosing a programme may differ in motivation, access or baseline mobility limitation. Those factors can also affect success. Filtering existing programme users leaves that selection process in place.

Randomizing the offer can help estimate its effect under the study conditions. If some people do not take up the offer, the effect of actual use is a different question. A new programme version or population also needs separate evidence and assumptions.

An intervention actively sets a treatment. Selecting records of people who already received it leaves their original assignment process in place. Specify the treatment, alternative, target population, outcome and follow-up. Assignment and actual use can differ: some people may not take up their assigned option. Randomization applies to assignment; comparing actual users may bring their own choices back into the comparison.
A historical or before-and-after comparison does not automatically reproduce random assignment; time and the people included may also differ.
Name the assigned change, its alternative, the people and the outcome time.
Random assignment changes how the specified reminder is assigned. The other plans compare existing choices or different time periods; neither sets a new assignment rule.
Sorting existing users or comparing years does not change their original assignment process. Which plan does?
Which plan decides how reminders are assigned, rather than sorting people by an earlier choice?
A clinic has records of patients who chose to turn on appointment reminders. Which plan would actively assign reminders?
Random assignment changes how the specified reminder is assigned. The other plans compare existing choices or different time periods; neither sets a new assignment rule.

The study randomizes who receives the offer, not who takes it up. People decide whether to use the support, so comparing actual users can answer a different question. A future policy or population would also define a different target.
The assigned offer, later use and a future policy are different targets. Which one did this study randomize?
Was the offer randomized, or was later use randomized?

A hospital offers transport support at random. Some patients who receive the offer do not use it. The study measures attendance over 30 days. Which effect is the randomized comparison designed to estimate?

The study randomizes who receives the offer, not who takes it up. People decide whether to use the support, so comparing actual users can answer a different question. A future policy or population would also define a different target.

Consider two hypothetical people on a score where higher is better. Compared with B, A would raise one person's score by 10 points and lower the other's by 2 points. Their average effect is +4 points, even though one person is harmed. These individual effects are given for the example; group averages alone would not reveal them.
Worked example
Define the mean outcome if the same target population were assigned A and if it were assigned B. This is different from comparing whichever people happened to choose each programme.
For the score example, 68 - 62 = +6 mobility-score points. For a binary outcome, 75% - 60% = +15 percentage points. The relative increase is 15/60 = 25%; these are different summaries.

A positive average can include people who benefit by different amounts, people who do not benefit and people who are harmed. A study based on a finite sample estimates that population contrast with uncertainty. Subtracting the sample means does not remove the uncertainty.

An average treatment effect compares mean outcomes under two interventions for the same target population. Subtract the comparison from the treatment and state the units. For a binary (yes/no) outcome, a probability difference uses percentage points, not a relative percentage. An individual's effect compares that person's outcome under A with their outcome under B. Group averages do not reveal that pair for each person. Even with a positive average, some people may see no benefit or be harmed. Sampling uncertainty means another sample could give a different estimate.
A percentage-point difference is not a relative percentage, and an average does not identify each person's response.
Report A minus B, its units, the target population and the follow-up.
68 - 62 = +6 mobility-score points. This is the average six-week score difference for the eligible study population. It is neither a relative percentage nor an individual effect.
Check the subtraction and keep the units as score points. A group average does not tell you each participant's response.
Calculate the difference between the two means. Does that number describe the group average or every participant?

Eligible participants are randomly assigned A or B. Their mean scores at six weeks are 68 and 62 mobility-score points, respectively. For this calculation, ignore sampling uncertainty. What is A minus B?
68 - 62 = +6 mobility-score points. This is the average six-week score difference for the eligible study population. It is neither a relative percentage nor an individual effect.

Each participant was assigned one programme. These results do not show how that same person would have done under the other programme. The group rates estimate an average difference with uncertainty; they do not identify who benefited, saw no benefit or was harmed.
A difference between groups does not reveal each person's two possible outcomes. Check whether the answer claims to know everyone's response or the identities of those who benefited.
Do the two group rates show how the same person would have done under both assignments?

A randomized study records recovery by day 30 in 54/100 people assigned A and 40/100 assigned B. A has the higher group recovery rate. What can these results tell us about any one patient's benefit from A rather than B?

Each participant was assigned one programme. These results do not show how that same person would have done under the other programme. The group rates estimate an average difference with uncertainty; they do not identify who benefited, saw no benefit or was harmed.

Baseline mobility limitation can influence both programme choice and later success. The overall A and B groups may therefore contain different starting conditions. Suppose a programme changes practice time, which then affects success. Practice time is a mediator in this model. The programme's total effect includes this pathway. Adjusting for practice time would block it.
Worked example

If baseline mobility limitation affects choice and success, pooling all A records and all B records can mix programme differences with differences in who chose each programme. A stratum is a group with the same specified baseline category.

In a separate worked example, A/B success rates are 80%/70% in the lower-baseline group and 50%/40% in the higher-baseline group. With a half-and-half target, A is 0.5 x 80% + 0.5 x 50% = 65%; B is 55%. The contrast is +10 percentage points.

The pre-treatment variables must remove confounding; both treatments must occur in each relevant group; treatment versions must be consistent. Do not add every predictor. A mediator carries part of the treatment's effect; adjusting for it can remove that part. A collider is a common effect; conditioning on it can introduce bias.

Baseline means measured before treatment. Confounding occurs when a common cause affects treatment and outcome. Standardization compares rates within pre-treatment groups using the same target weights for both treatments; pooling keeps each selected group's own mixture. Causal interpretation requires no remaining confounding, overlap (both treatments possible) and consistency (well-defined treatment versions).
Weighting does not repair an omitted common cause or a group with no comparison treatment. A good outcome predictor is not automatically safe to adjust for.
Justify the baseline groups and use one target mixture for both alternatives.

Use each treatment's outcome rates within the pre-treatment groups and apply the same target weights to both. The causal interpretation requires adequate adjustment, overlap and consistency; calculating weights does not establish those assumptions.
Each selected group's own weights represent its own mixture, not one common target. Adding predictors also requires a causal reason; having more variables does not establish the assumptions.
Both treatment alternatives must describe the same target population, under the stated adjustment assumptions.

Baseline severity affects both treatment choice and recovery. Assume that adjusting for severity removes all confounding, that both treatments occur at each severity, and that treatment versions are consistent. How should we calculate the target-population comparison?

Use each treatment's outcome rates within the pre-treatment groups and apply the same target weights to both. The causal interpretation requires adequate adjustment, overlap and consistency; calculating weights does not establish those assumptions.

In this model, the later variable is a mediator through which part of the treatment's effect passes. Adjusting for it can block that part. This does not invalidate the stated adequate baseline set or make observational inference impossible.
A useful prediction does not by itself tell us what to adjust for. Check the effect being estimated and whether this variable carries part of it.
A mediator carries an effect from treatment to outcome. Check whether the proposed variable lies on that route.

We want the total effect of operation type on recovery. Assume baseline risk already controls confounding. In the proposed model, operation type affects infection, which affects recovery. Should we also adjust for infection just because it predicts recovery?

In this model, the later variable is a mediator through which part of the treatment's effect passes. Adjusting for it can block that part. This does not invalidate the stated adequate baseline set or make observational inference impossible.
A large registry can describe a group difference precisely while leaving its cause unresolved. A trial result can also be specific to the people, programme and follow-up studied.
Worked example

An effect is identified relative to a set of data and assumptions if every causal model compatible with them gives the same effect. Different models fitting the observations can otherwise imply different intervention effects.

Adjustment by baseline mobility limitation assumes no remaining confounding, both programmes possible in the relevant groups, and consistent versions. Random assignment can support an assignment-effect argument under its design and follow-up conditions. More records can reduce sampling error without repairing missing causal assumptions.

A different population, programme version or outcome time is a different target. Assess the evidence and assumptions for that target separately. Agreement between an adjusted estimate and a trial estimate does not prove every assumption, and missing follow-up can create another problem.

Identification asks whether the data and stated causal assumptions determine an effect. Estimation calculates it from a finite sample, with uncertainty. Transport asks whether the result applies to another population, treatment version or follow-up time, using evidence and assumptions for that new target. A precise estimate alone does not settle the other questions.
A narrow uncertainty interval is not proof that confounding is absent or that the effect transfers to a different setting.
State why the effect is identifiable, how uncertain its estimate is, and where it applies.

A large sample can reduce sampling error for the observed association. Without a design or assumptions that address the missing common cause, different intervention effects can still fit those records.
Precision and identification are different. Ask what assumption or design addresses the missing common cause, rather than how many rows are available.
More records can improve precision without resolving which causal explanation is right.
A registry has a million records of treatment and recovery. A missing factor may cause both. No other design for identifying the causal effect is given. What can the large sample tell us?

A large sample can reduce sampling error for the observed association. Without a design or assumptions that address the missing common cause, different intervention effects can still fit those records.

The trial supports its specified assignment comparison under the study's design conditions. Applying it to different people, treatment versions or follow-up times needs a separate argument and often more evidence.
A randomized result does not automatically cover a different target. Compare the new population, treatment and follow-up with those in the study.
Compare the proposed use with the population, treatment and follow-up actually studied.

A well-run randomized trial identifies the effect of assignment for eligible adults with complete follow-up. A team applies the result to children receiving a different dose and assessed later. What needs more evidence or assumptions?

The trial supports its specified assignment comparison under the study's design conditions. Applying it to different people, treatment versions or follow-up times needs a separate argument and often more evidence.

Each pooled average uses its programme group's own baseline mixture. Standardization applies the same target weights to both programmes. A causal interpretation still requires adequate pre-treatment adjustment, overlap and consistency. Read the numerical results from your saved runs.

Pooled rates can combine programme outcome differences with differences in who chose each programme. Weighting still relies on the causal assumptions; the calculation does not check whether they hold.
Compare how much each baseline group contributes to each programme's average in both calculations.

You compared the pooled result with the common-target result. Why can the A-minus-B contrast change?

workbench.title: Programme practice 1 of 4
workbench.introduction: A rehabilitation service is comparing six-week programmes A and B for eligible rehabilitation patients. Success means reaching the declared mobility target at six weeks. Before the programme, people have lower or higher mobility limitation. People who choose A can differ from people who choose B before either programme starts. In this teaching model, success rates within those starting groups stay fixed while you change one part of the comparison at a time.

guide.parameter_description: Start with people choosing, then change only to balanced random assignment. Keep a target where 80% of people have higher mobility limitation, and use common target weights for A and B. The model keeps its within-group success rules fixed. Matching adjusted results do not establish that a real study has measured every relevant common cause.
guide.goal: Separate a calculation under supplied assumptions from evidence that those assumptions hold.
guide.story: A rehabilitation service is comparing six-week programmes A and B for eligible rehabilitation patients. Success means reaching the declared mobility target at six weeks. Before the programme, people have lower or higher mobility limitation. People who choose A can differ from people who choose B before either programme starts. In this teaching model, success rates within those starting groups stay fixed while you change one part of the comparison at a time. For the last comparison, keep one target population and inspect both the overall and common-target differences.
guide.prediction_prompt: When you change assignment and keep the target weights fixed, which difference do you expect to change: the overall comparison, the target comparison, or both?
guide.comparison_prompt: Compare both differences under the two assignment rules. Why doesn't agreement in this teaching model show that a real study has no remaining confounding?
